newsitem.title: FINLAND: UPM's Canada plans logical - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UPM's Canada plans logical - analysts.

text.p: Acquiring paper-making capacity in Canada would be a logical step for Finnish forest industry group UPM-Kymmene Oy, analysts said on Tuesday in the wake of news UPM had bid for Canadian Repap Enterprises Inc.

"UPM has said earlier that ... when there are only a few paper producers left in the world, they plan to be one of the big ones -- and that requires production on other continents," said Gustav Lucander, analyst at Aros Securities.
UPM executive vice president Martin Granholm on Tuesday confirmed a media report that UPM had bid for parts of Repap, but said the bid had become void when Repap got another offer.
Finnish business daily Kauppalehti said UPM was likely to bid for Repap if merger talks between Repap and another Canadian paper maker, Avenor Inc, failed.
"What may possibly be on its way we will return to at a later stage," Granholm told Reuters, but did not elaborate.

Repap has an annual output capacity of one million tonnes of coated paper, 685,000 tonnes of northern bleached softwood kraft pulp, 125,000 tonnes of magnesium bisulphate hardwood pulp, 170,000 tonnes of kraft paper and 542 million board feet of lumber.
In January, Repap reported a 1996 pre-tax loss of 484.5 million Canadian dollars against a profit of 169.7 million in 1995, and net sales of 1.7 billion Canadian dollars, down 17 percent on 1995.
"(Repap) is on the right continent," said Paivi Palomaki, analyst at Aktia Bank.
"UPM has said it is interested in the North American market -- Asia too, but I have understood that they are now more interested in North America."
As Europe's biggest forestry group, UPM-Kymmene could soon run up against limits to expansion in Europe, analysts said.
"The company's opportunties to expand further in Europe are limited. There, they have achieved almost everything that can be achieved in terms of market share," Palomaki said.

"I think the market's first reaction (to an acquisition by UPM of Repap) would probably be positive ... The market considers it much better for UPM to expand through acquisitions than to set up its own production capacity," Opstock Securities analyst Jukka Linden said.
"UPM is the most international of Finland's forestry groups, but the trend is towards locating production plants closer to the markets," said one analyst, speaking anonymously.
A possible link-up with Repap would fit well with UPM's product palette, analysts said.

UPM is the world's biggest coated magazine paper producer with an annual output capacity of 1.83 million tonnes and also the biggest producer of super-calendered (SC) paper with 1.23 million tonnes. UPM's total magazine paper output was 2.46 million tonnes in 1996.

"UPM is strong in magazine paper production, and so this would represent their core competence area," Linden said, adding that UPM should be well placed to judge the value of the operations in question.

"They (UPM) don't have any liquidity troubles that would prevent a deal from being arranged in a way that would satisfy the market," one analyst said when asked how UPM would fund such an acquisition.
But analysts said they would need to know more details of a possible offer for the debt-burdened Repap before they could say how well the deal would be viewed by the market in the long term.
Repap and Avenor shareholders are scheduled to vote on March 26 on the proposed merger.
